


Plant Vogtle Units 3 &amp; 4

Fifth Semi-Annual 
Construction Monitoring Report

August 2011

Docket No. 29849


EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 


This is the fifth semi-annual Vogtle Construction Monitoring (“VCM”) report (“Fifth VCM Report”) submitted by Georgia Power Company (“Georgia Power” or the “Company”) to the Georgia Public Service Commission (the “Commission”) pursuant to the stipulation (the “Stipulation”) adopted in the Commission’s order in Docket No. 27800 (the “Certification Order”).  

The executive summary of the Fifth VCM Report is as follows:
This Project is on track and the targets are achievable.  The Plant Vogtle Units 3 and 4 project (the “Project”) is moving forward towards issuance of the Vogtle combined construction and operating license (“COL”) around the end of 2011 with Unit 3 becoming operational in 2016 and Unit 4 in 2017.  
The Company is being accountable to our customers.  As discussed in Item 14 herein, completion of Units 3 and 4 at Plant Vogtle (the “Units”) is significantly less expensive than any of the available alternatives.
The Company is in position to deliver to its customers nearly $1 billion dollars in benefits as a result of the Company’s pursuit of the U.S. Department of Energy (“DOE”) loan guarantee (“Loan Guarantee”) and the production tax credits (“PTCs”), and as a result of the Commission’s approval of early recovery of construction work in progress (“CWIP”) in rate base. 

As with each of our previous VCM reports, the Project remains on schedule and under budget and the economics continue to improve relative to the assumptions made at the time the Units were certified (“Certification”).  In this Fifth VCM Report, the Company requests that the Commission verify and approve the construction expenditures for the Project during the reporting period of January 1, 2011 through June 30, 2011 (the “Reporting Period”).  This Fifth VCM Report provides the basis upon which the Commission may verify and approve such expenditures as made pursuant to the certificate in accordance with O.C.G.A. § 46-3A-7(b).  In addition, the Company’s semi-annual reports generally provide the basis by which the Commission may approve, disapprove, or modify any proposed revisions in the Project schedule and budget; however, the Company is not requesting any changes to the overall Project schedule or budget for this Reporting Period.  

In addition to summarizing the information contained in this Fifth VCM Report, this executive summary also highlights several key developments and issues that occurred during the Reporting Period to put the progress of the Project in context.  

Construction of the Units is tracking under the $6.113 billion certified amount (the “Revised Certified Amount”).  There continues to be pressure on both the Project schedule and cost, and the Company continues to manage both.  As discussed in Item 9, there are new projected costs related to Project oversight, including costs related to operational readiness, quality and compliance, start up, and labor related expenses. There have also been emerging cost savings that offset some of those increases. Most importantly, as stated above, there are significant savings for customers as a result of the Company’s pursuit of the DOE Loan Guarantee and the PTCs, and as a result of the Commission’s approval of early recovery of CWIP in rate base. The Company’s current projections show that these savings have the equivalent effect of reducing the total cost impact of the Project on customers by nearly $1 billion dollars in benefits to customers. The Company believes that when the Project is completed, and all costs and other savings are considered, the Project will have a more favorable impact on customers than was projected at Certification.

The original Project schedule approved in the Certification Order provides for a commercial operation date (“COD”) for Unit 3 of April 1, 2016 and a COD for Unit 4 of April 1, 2017. In the Fourth VCM Report, the Company reported that the Unit 3 COD was projected for June 7, 2016.  During the Fifth Reporting Period, on May 27, 2011, Westinghouse Electric Company, LLC (“Westinghouse”) and Stone &amp; Webster, Inc. (together with Westinghouse, the “Consortium”) issued an updated integrated project schedule (the “Integrated Project Schedule”) that included a schedule compression that returns the Unit 3 COD to April 1, 2016.  These types of fluctuations may occur with a project of this magnitude, however, the Consortium and the Company will continually assess known schedule fluctuations for any potential future impacts on the target COD dates.  

During the Reporting Period, there was progress made in the licensing of the Units. As discussed in detail in Item 10, the design control document (“DCD”) Revision 18 was submitted to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (“NRC”) at the end of the Fourth VCM reporting period (on December 2, 2010) and the Company submitted the COL application (“COLA”) revision, which incorporated these DCD revisions, to the NRC on January 23, 2011. DCD Revision 19 was submitted to the NRC on June 13, 2011 and the Company submitted the conforming COLA revision on June 24, 2011. The completion of the COLA review remains dependent on the NRC’s review of the DCD. Although outside this Reporting Period, on August 2, 2011, the NRC issued a letter outlining the revised safety review schedule that supports the issuance of a Final Safety Evaluation Report (“FSER”) in August 2011, and subsequently, the NRC issued the DCD FSER on August 5, 2011. The NRC has indicated that the target date for completion of the mandatory hearing, including issuance of a final NRC decision on the COLs, is December 2011. This assumes that the AP1000 design certification amendment rulemaking is completed.  The Company continues to anticipate the issuance of the COLs in December 2011 or early 2012.

As discussed in Item 12, the Company continues to conduct surveillance and closely monitor the audit and vendor issues with Shaw Modular Solutions (“SMS”).  In the Fourth VCM Report, the Company provided preliminary information concerning an NRC inspection and the resulting requirements that SMS develop a comprehensive plan to address nuclear safety culture, quality assurance effectiveness, application and understanding of nuclear fundamentals and the continuous process improvement culture. During the Reporting Period, the NRC attempted to conduct an inspection of the SMS facility on January 10, 2011, but was unable to complete it due to the lack of actual production work at the site.  Since that time, SMS has demonstrated significant progress in implementing its improvement plan and, as a result, on April 28, Shaw removed the restrictions placed on SMS on December 20, 2010 for module fabrication or rework activities. The Company also continues to monitor vendor issues with Chicago Bridge and Iron (“CB&amp;I”). CB&amp;I, which was under a Stop Work Order (“SWO”) issued on October 24, 2010, was allowed to restart work in a phased approach and showed tremendous improvement in following work instructions and procedures.  Although outside the Reporting Period, CB&amp;I was fully released from the SWO on July 31, 2011. 

Finally, as discussed above and in Item 14, completion of the Units is significantly less expensive than any of the available alternatives. Table 14.1 below shows the difference in lifetime costs of building, operating and maintaining the gas-fired combined cycle (“CC”) alternative less the lifetime costs of completing, operating, and maintaining the Units over the same useful life of 60 years, with positive savings meaning the Units are less expensive to customers than the gas-fired CC alternative.  All twelve scenarios shown in the current economic analysis report positive benefits to customers if the Units are completed.  In addition, Table 14.2 shows the results of the breakeven analysis that calculates the maximum capital expenditures that could be spent to complete the Units and maintain lifetime costs that are equal to the cost of the gas-fired CC alternative.  In all scenarios, the maximum capital cost to complete the Units exceeds the Company’s current estimate of the cost to complete the Units (including marginal construction financing costs).

The Commission staff (“Staff”) and the Construction Monitor have been kept abreast of the progress of construction, and the issues discussed above, as well as those discussed throughout this Fifth VCM Report, through monthly meetings with Georgia Power, and through their review of the Level 1 schedule and the Vogtle 3 and 4 Project Metrics Packages. While the Project continues to track under the Revised Certified Amount, as with any project of this magnitude, the cost of several individual items will be greater than budgeted while the cost of others will be less than budgeted. However, as stated above, when the overall net change of these items is considered, together with the impact of the costs savings of the Loan Guarantee, PTCs and CWIP in rate base, the overall impact of the Project is more favorable for customers than originally anticipated at the time of Certification.

In conclusion, the Company is currently managing pressures on both the Project schedule and cost, and will continue to do both while expanding its oversight efforts.  Currently, the Total Current Forecast is less than the Revised Certified Amount; therefore, the Company does not request an adjustment to the Revised Certified Amount at this time.  The Company requests that the Commission verify and approve the construction expenditures incurred during the Fifth VCM Reporting Period.





As agreed in the Stipulation that was incorporated into the Certification Order, the Company responds to the 15 specified items in the order in which they appear in Section 2(d)(1-15) of the Stipulation as follows:

The reasons for any additional change in the estimated costs of the units since the process began.

For purposes of this Reporting Period, the Company reports against a total Revised Certified Amount of $6.113 billion.  The effective impact of the capital cost is less than it was projected to be at the time of Certification due to the beneficial impact of the Loan Guarantee and PTCs.  The original $6.4 billion certified amount has already been reduced to $6.113 billion to reflect the Commission’s order to allow for early recovery of CWIP in rate base.  The cost reports are provided in Tables 1.1 and 1.1a below.

A description of any cooperative actions between other builders of nuclear units in the southeast to address labor, crafts, engineering and management requirements. 

Southern Nuclear (“SNC”) cooperates with other builders and potential builders of nuclear units to address engineering and management requirements via industry related groups. These groups provide forums for builders and potential builders of a given technology type to consider issues common to the participants, including development of training, procedures and programs.  The groups operate under strict antitrust rules and do not collaborate in any way to influence the labor markets. 

As a member of NuStart, SNC is engaged with other NuStart members (DTE Energy, Duke Energy, EDF International North America, Inc., Entergy Nuclear, Exelon Corporation, Nextera Energy, Progress Energy, SCANA Corporation, and Tennessee Valley Authority) to support the following activities:

Engineering and design document reviews with Westinghouse to support design finalization efforts and promote standardization of site specific design.
As the Reference COL Applicant, NuStart provides licensing support to SNC in addressing standard COLA licensing items including preparations for the first annual Final Safety Analysis Report (“FSAR”) update, technical specification upgrades and commitment tracking support.

As a member of APOG LLC (“APOG”), SNC has engaged with other APOG members (Progress Energy Carolinas, Duke Energy Carolinas, Florida Power &amp; Light and South Carolina Electric and Gas Company (“SCE&amp;G”)) to support the following activities either through financial means or with participation:

Development of a knowledge and abilities (K&amp;A) catalog that provides the basis for the NRC licensed operator training and examinations throughout the life of the plant. This document has been submitted to the NRC on behalf of the industry.
Review of Westinghouse procedures and development of a standard set of operation and maintenance procedures that will be proposed to all AP1000 utilities.
Review of engineering and design issues with Westinghouse to resolve common problems for the benefit of all AP1000 owners.
Review of the final layout of the plant to ensure it meets regulatory requirements and industry expectations for constructability, operability, maintainability, inspectability and testability.
Development, together with APOG member utilities, Westinghouse and the NRC, of human factors programs associated with man machine interface and procedure usage protocols. The computerized procedure system presents some opportunities to rethink traditional methods that could simplify communications, reduce potential human errors and enhance safe operations.
Review of the Westinghouse and Shaw lessons learned program to ensure lessons learned from China and other AP1000 utilities are reviewed and, if needed, incorporated into the design.
Hiring a full time APOG Programs Manager to manage the development of programs necessary for testing, start-up and eventual operation of the AP1000. These programs range from engineering programs to maintenance, chemistry, health physics, operations, Occupational Safety and Health Administration compliance, etc., as related to the AP1000.
Supporting standard aspects of licensing and licensing compliance. 
Coordinating, through the APOG Quality Assurance Committee, the QA surveillance activities of major vendors and sub-tier suppliers. In addition, the APOG QA Committee members, along with Westinghouse and Shaw Quality Assurance management, participating in quarterly meetings to assure the independent quality organizations in each of the companies are aligned.

SNC, in cooperation with SCE&amp;G, has contracted with Westinghouse for initial training program development, instruction, and certification of utility licensed operator instructors.  The first two groups of 48 instructors (24 each from SCE&amp;G and SNC) completed nine weeks of initial training in 2010.  Although outside the Reporting Period additional operations instructor training will take place at Westinghouse facilities in late 2011 and early 2012. This training will consist of 15 weeks of training sequentially for two groups of 12 instructors on the AP1000 control room simulator. This training completes the last phase of certifying SNC instructors to teach licensed operator candidates.

REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED    REDACTED    REDACTED    REDACTED    REDACTED

In addition to the items listed above, SNC continues to participate in leadership roles for various Nuclear Energy Institute (“NEI”) sponsored groups, specifically, the Design Centered Working Group (“DCWG”), the New Plant Working Group (“NPWG”) and the New Plant Oversight Committee (“NPOC”).  The DCWG, formed by NEI at the request of the NRC, is made up of the AP1000 utilities with the purpose of standardizing licensing activities associated with the DCD, the COL and construction of the AP1000.  The NPWG, managed by NEI, is a policy-making group that establishes guidance for addressing the NRC, legislative and public affair issues for new reactors (e.g. AP1000, ESBWR) and modular reactors. The direction for the NPWG is established by the NPOC, which is made up of nuclear industry executives.

At the close of 2010, SNC opened a representative office in Shanghai.  The Shanghai project manager focuses on maintaining and strengthening relationships with the owner companies and the operating companies of the four AP1000 units currently under construction at Sanmen Nuclear Power Station and Haiyang Nuclear Power Plant.  The construction efforts at all four Chinese units are approximately 24 months ahead of the Vogtle Project and, therefore, are rich sources of lessons learned for the Units’ construction and subsequent operation.  The Shanghai project manager routinely travels between the two China sites to monitor progress against a published milestone schedule to pinpoint opportunities for construction observations.  During the Reporting Period, the Shanghai project manager met with Sanmen representatives to understand the integral steps and durations involved in preparing and pouring the Nuclear Island concrete layers. At Sanmen, he also observed and obtained details regarding the design and use of a temporary cover for the containment vessel top head that protects the contents of the containment vessel from weather and at Haiyang, he observed the setting of the CA03. 

An explanation of how the indices used in the EPC contract are tracking.

On February 22, 2010, the Consortium and Georgia Power, acting for itself and as agent for Oglethorpe Power Corporation, Municipal Electric Authority of Georgia and the City of Dalton (the “Owners”) entered into Amendment No. 3 to the Engineering Procurement and Construction (“EPC”) Agreement.  Amendment No. 3, which was approved by the Commission on August 17, 2010, replaces certain index-based adjustments to the purchase price with fixed escalation amounts.  This means commodity and inflation risks have been significantly reduced, and the risk of higher than anticipated escalation is shifted from the Company’s customers to the Consortium.

With Amendment No. 3 in place, the only remaining index is the REDACTED Index, which is currently tracking REDACTED original estimates on a cumulative basis, as shown in Table 3.1. Table 3.1 

Any updated estimate of on site spent fuel storage costs, including the costs for dry storage of spent fuel for an extended period of time after shutdown, and any updated calculation of spent fuel storage costs assuming Yucca Mountain is never available. 

As previously reported, the Company provided a sensitivity analysis for spent fuel storage costs to the  Staff and the Independent Evaluator in October 2008 that estimated the cost of on-site storage through 2088, which is ten years beyond the anticipated shutdown of Unit 4.  There is no change at this time to the estimate provided in October 2008.  In November 2008, SNC executed a contract with the DOE that requires the DOE to complete removal of spent fuel from the Units within ten years from the date of the shutdown of Unit 4.

As reported in the Fourth VCM Report, President Obama asked the U.S. Secretary of Energy to establish a 15 member “Blue Ribbon Commission on America’s Nuclear Future,” charged with addressing long-term storage and disposal options for spent nuclear fuel. The three Blue Ribbon Commission subcommittees issued draft reports in late Spring 2011 to recommend policy and legislative changes to address alternative storage options, spent fuel recycling and disposal options. The various subcommittees recommended, among other things, that the United States expeditiously develop one or more interim and permanent storage facilities for the safe disposal of high-level nuclear waste, as well as the creation of a new, single purpose organization to develop and implement a focused, integrated program for the transportation, storage and disposal of nuclear waste in the U.S. The final reports from the subcommittees are expected to be issued on January 29, 2012. Until any recommendations are implemented, there is no change in the expected spent fuel storage costs. 

The status of the Company’s loan guarantee application at the Department of Energy and to the extent that application is granted, then the Company shall also report on the impact it has or would have on the final expected in-service cost of the units. 
There has been no change in the status of the Company’s conditional commitment for a Loan Guarantee from the DOE that would apply to future Company borrowings related to the Units since the last reporting period.  Total guaranteed borrowings will not exceed 70 percent of eligible Project costs, or approximately $3.4 billion. 

Final approval and issuance of the Loan Guarantee is subject to receipt of the COLs from the NRC, negotiation of definitive agreements (that will conclude following receipt of the COLs), completion of due diligence by the DOE, and receipt of any necessary regulatory approvals or conditions as defined in the definitive agreements. 

As a result of the Loan Guarantee, Georgia Power and its customers are currently expected to save approximately $15 million to $20 million in interest costs annually, at the corporate level, over the expected life of the bonds.  The actual amount of the interest savings will depend on the final terms and the timing of the specific borrowings.  

The estimated impact of the DOE Loan Guarantee on this Project is reflected in financing costs in Tables 1.1, 1.1a, and 8.1. The portion of the estimated net benefits of the Loan Guarantee that is allocated to the Project has been reflected in the Total Current Forecast based on the information available at this time.  Discussion with the DOE on this topic is ongoing.  Additional costs associated with compliance with applicable federal regulations pertaining to the acceptance of a Loan Guarantee may be identified and incorporated at a later date.

The status of the Company’s combined construction and operating license (COL) application at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. 

The most recent licensing schedule is shown in Table 10.1 below. 
 
Significant progress continues to be made in the licensing of the Units. As noted in the Fourth VCM Report, the DCD Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (“ACRS”) Full Committee review was held on December 2, 2010, and a subsequent ACRS Full Committee letter was issued on December 13, 2010, which supported the issuance of the design certification.  Additionally, the ACRS Full Committee issued letters on December 20, 2010 and January 19, 2011 supporting the resolution of the design issues on long-term core cooling and aircraft impact assessment, respectively.  On a parallel schedule, ACRS Subcommittee meetings were held throughout the latter half of 2010 on the Vogtle COLA with the recommendation of the ACRS Subcommittee on December 17, 2010 that the COLs should be issued as well.  The ACRS Full Committee issued a letter endorsing the Vogtle COLA on January 24, 2011. 
 
While the NRC staff and the ACRS had resolved the technical issues in the DCD and the COLA last year, conforming changes to the DCD and the COLA had to be made to incorporate those resolutions.  DCD Revision 18 was submitted to the NRC on December 2, 2010, and the COLA revision that incorporated that DCD revision was submitted to the NRC on January 23, 2011.  During the course of the NRC’s confirmatory review of DCD Revision 18, issues were identified where the information was not incorporated as the NRC expected.  These remaining issues were resolved with the NRC staff in parallel to the DCD Amendment proposed rulemaking noticing and public comment period.  The proposed rule was noticed February 24, 2011 and the comment period ended May 10, 2011, and it drew several public comments that are still in the process of being resolved.  The three key issues that arose from the DCD Revision 18 confirmatory review were related to seismic methods used to evaluate the Passive Core Cooling Water Storage Tank, use of load combinations on the shield building, and the calculation of the peak containment pressure. These issues were resolved and incorporated in the DCD Revision 19 submittal on June 13, 2011.  The conforming COLA revision incorporating DCD Revision 19 was submitted to the NRC on June 24, 2011.  

Separate from the DCD revision process, the NRC also conducted additional inspections and audits of the aircraft impact analysis.  Westinghouse completed the additional analyses on July 25, 2011.  After an NRC review of these analyses to assure that the results met NRC expectations, the DCD FSER was approved on July 29, 2011. This additional work did not impact the overall rulemaking schedule.

The completion of the COLA review remains dependent on the NRC’s review of the DCD.  The NRC issued the final supplemental environmental impact statement (FSEIS) for the COLs on March 31, 2011. 

Although outside the Reporting Period, on August 2, 2011, the NRC issued a letter outlining the revised safety review schedule that supports the issuance of the COL FSER in August 2011, and subsequently, the NRC issued the DCD FSER on August 5, 2011. The NRC has indicated that the target date for completion of the mandatory hearing, including issuance of a final NRC decision on the COLs, is December 2011. This assumes that the AP1000 design certification amendment rulemaking is completed. 

Finally, as previously reported, the NRC has yet to rule on the appeal filed on December 9, 2010 by petitioners who sought to intervene in the COLA process.  On August 13, 2010, the NRC received a new petition concerning the inspection programs and the coatings for the containment vessel.  The Atomic Safety and Licensing Board (“ASLB”) convened, considered, and subsequently dismissed the petition on November 30, 2010 but has not yet ruled on the petitioners’ appeal of the dismissal.

On April 14, 2011, 47 organizations and individuals filed a petition before the NRC in the Vogtle COLA proceeding, as well as 22 other licensing and relicensing dockets, requesting that the NRC suspend all licensing proceedings and the AP1000 design certification rulemaking. The petitioners argued that the NRC should not issue new plant licenses or license renewals until its regulatory review of the events in Japan is complete and requested modified procedures to allow intervenors to raise contentions after the NRC released its final findings regarding the Japan events.   SNC responded on May 2, 2011, asserting that the requested suspension was not justified under NRC precedent, and that the petition did not meet the requirements for any admissible filing in the Vogtle proceeding. NRC staff and NEI also opposed the filing.  The NRC Commission’s decision on the petition is pending.

The status of procurement, engineering, fabrication, transportation and erection of major equipment. 

Consortium Responsibilities.  There is no change to this item since the Fourth VCM Report.  Under the EPC Agreement, the Consortium has the responsibility for all activities involving the procurement, engineering, fabrication, transportation and erection of major equipment.  Georgia Power, through its agent SNC, is overseeing those activities to confirm that the Consortium is abiding by the terms of the EPC Agreement and that the Project meets the standards of quality demanded by Georgia Power. 

Procurement.   The June 2011 EPC Monthly Status Report and June 2011 Vogtle 3 and 4 Project Metrics Package provide more detailed information regarding the status of procurement.  In summary, according to the June 2011 EPC Monthly Status Report, Westinghouse and Shaw have issued 250 purchase orders (“POs”) as compared to the 236 POs that were planned.  In addition to the information presented by the Consortium, the Company also tracks planned versus actual procurement activities for major components through its Vendor Surveillance Organization.  At this time, all of the planned major components POs have been issued for the Project.

The Company continues to conduct surveillance and closely monitor the audit and vendor issues with SMS.  As reported in the Fourth VCM Report, REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTEDREDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED. On January 10, 2011, the NRC attempted to conduct an inspection of the SMS facility but was unable to complete it due to the lack of actual production work at the site. Subsequently, the NRC requested an action plan and Shaw Nuclear, SMS, and Westinghouse jointly developed a comprehensive plan to address concerns regarding nuclear safety culture, SMS quality assurance effectiveness, application and understanding of nuclear fundamentals, and the continuous process improvement culture.  The Consortium increased its presence and level of quality assurance and quality oversight at the SMS facility.  SMS has demonstrated significant progress in implementing its improvement plan. As a result, on April 28, 2011 Shaw removed restrictions for module fabrication or rework activities from SMS that has been imposed on December 20, 2010. The Company’s senior executives continue to hold weekly meetings with the Consortium’s senior management to receive updates on its ongoing progress to resolve any quality concerns.  

The Company also continues to closely monitor the vendor issues with CB&amp;I. As previously reported in the Fourth VCM Report, an SWO was issued to CB&amp;I on October 24, 2010. The SWO required the following actions prior to the restart of work: (1) acceptance of the response to the Westinghouse Supplier Corrective Action Request (“SCAR”); (2) approval of a root cause analysis; (3) completion of a quality program audit of CB&amp;I at the site by Westinghouse; and (4) completion of the development, training and implementation of a Human Performance Program.  The SCAR was formally closed on January 13, 2011, after Westinghouse received a satisfactory response. Westinghouse revised the CB&amp;I SWO to allow for a phased approach to the restart activities. CB&amp;I’s root cause analysis was formally approved on January 28, 2011 by the Westinghouse Quality Managers and Root Cause Analyst. A follow-up site audit was conducted during the week of February 28, 2011, which resulted in eleven new findings that were resolved prior to releasing CB&amp;I for the limited restart in May 2011. Westinghouse issued the CB&amp;I Human Performance Procedure on November 30, 2010. With these actions complete, the limited restart (for Phase 1 activities) occurred in early May. CB&amp;I was released to perform Phase 2 scope work and the Phase 3 readiness review was completed on June 23, 2011. CB&amp;I is progressing through the phased restart approach having shown tremendous improvement in following work instructions and procedures. Although outside this Reporting Period, CB&amp;I was released for Phase 3 scope work on July 15, 2011, and full release of the SWO was issued on July 31, 2011.   

Also during the Reporting Period, issues with other subcontractors were identified and are being monitored.  Specifically, fabrication activities and delivery schedules were impacted by Mangiarotti sub-supplier issues such that REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED.  

Also during the Reporting Period, Doosan Heavy Industries (“Doosan”) continued fabrication of the Reactor Vessel. Equipment being manufactured in Japan is being closely monitored to determine any future schedule impacts as a result of the earthquake, although at this time none have been identified. Finally, Westinghouse issued an SWO to SPX, the squib valve manufacturer, in April 2011 and the SWO was lifted for manufacturing and procurement activities on May 6, 2011.  There have been no schedule impacts identified as a result of the SWO.

An updated comparison of the economics of the certified project to other capacity options.

The relative economic value for the Units can be determined by comparing the costs associated with completing, operating, and maintaining the Units over their 60 year useful life with the costs to build, operate, and maintain a gas-fired CC unit over a comparable time period, which is the next most viable generation alternative over the same period.  The economic analysis performed for this Fifth VCM Report has relied on the methodologies used in all previous economic evaluations conducted in Docket Nos. 27800 and 29849.

The economic evaluation presented in this Fifth VCM Report is based on the same underlying major planning assumptions used in the Fourth VCM Report with the exception of the load forecast. Updated load forecast information is not typically available to the Company for inclusion in the August filing due to the timing of our normal forecasting and planning process. However, the Company received updated economic indicators in December 2010 that suggested future GDP growth was expected to increase and would likely result in significant variances from the previous load forecast utilized in the Fourth VCM Report.  Due to these expected significant variances, the Company developed a new load forecast, communicated the results to Staff, and included the updated load forecast in this Fifth VCM Report.  Consistent with the Fourth VCM Report, a range of planning scenarios was used to evaluate the possible impacts of varying fuel and carbon prices.  Three possible fuel price forecasts were used as well as three possible carbon price cases ($0, $10, and $20 per ton of CO2) along with a policy case of $30/ton.  The fuel forecast is based on the Company’s B2011 fuel forecast and is consistent with the fuel forecast used in the Fourth VCM Report.  Carbon prices are per ton in REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED.

The estimate of the capital cost to complete the Units has been updated from the Fourth VCM Report along with pre-COD Operations and Maintenance (“O&amp;M”), post-COD O&amp;M and post-COD ongoing capital additions for the Units.  Projected decommissioning costs, spent fuel storage cost estimates, and the assumed operating characteristics of the Units have not changed.  The long-term marginal financing rates for debt and preferred stock have been updated to reflect current expectations.  Although not included in the economic evaluation, it is important to recognize that the Company currently estimates the net benefits to customers associated with the expected DOE Loan Guarantee would reduce the Company’s overall financing cost, over the life of the debt, by more than $350 million.  Furthermore, consistent with the Fourth VCM Report, the current economic evaluation assumes 50 percent of potential available PTCs, or $390 million.  On a combined basis, these incentives from the federal government, which the Company has worked to ensure, are available to the Project will provide an economic benefit to the Company’s customers in excess of $740 million, on a nominal basis.

“Sunk costs” (non-refundable capital and financing costs already incurred or projected to have been incurred as of August 31, 2011) are excluded from this forward-looking analysis. The current forecast of construction and capital costs as shown in Table 1.1, net of sunk costs, is used as the basis to determine “cost to complete.” Also, for purposes of this economic evaluation, the marginal financing costs being used are higher than current estimates of embedded average financing costs. Other references to financing costs in this Fifth VCM Report are based on estimates of embedded average financing costs.

The relative economics for the Units, when compared to the gas-fired CC alternative, vary depending on the assumptions for future fuel prices as well as with the projected carbon prices associated with potential future carbon legislation.  Compared to the results presented in the Fourth VCM Report, the benefits to customers of completing the Units have improved in all twelve scenarios.  This is primarily a result of the reduction in capital costs to complete the Units, as compared to the capital costs to complete the Units assumed in the Fourth VCM Report.  Table 14.1 below shows the difference between the lifetime costs of building, operating, and maintaining the gas-fired CC alternative and the Units, with positive savings meaning the Units are less expensive to customers than the gas-fired CC alternative.  All twelve scenarios show positive benefits to customers for completing and operating the Units.  

The Company has given considerable thought to assigning weights to the various scenarios and has concluded that because of the high degree of uncertainty during the next 67 years regarding the myriad of variables underlying each scenario, equal weighting should continue to be given to each scenario. The economic scenario results contemplate a vast range of key variables, such as future environmental regulations, possible climate change legislation, fuel prices and demand levels, potential federal portfolio requirements, federal policies toward new nuclear, the breadth and rate of expansion of new nuclear in the United States, and the interplay of other market forces.  Equal weightings are appropriate for each scenario because this method acknowledges the uncertainty inherent in making predictions regarding numerous variables over such a long planning horizon. The entire purpose of evaluating numerous scenarios is to assess the overall economics of a project in an uncertain future.  What may appear to be a “more likely” scenario today may appear to be “unlikely” tomorrow.  In the future, if some of the considerations underlying each economic scenario are further clarified and much more certain, the Company would assess the scenarios being contemplated and the appropriateness of equal weights for each scenario. However, the Company firmly believes that application of equal weightings to all scenarios is most appropriate at this time.  As such, the weighted average expected value of the relative savings for completion of the Units as compared to the gas-fired CC alternative is approximately $REDACTED.

The analyses provided in Tables 14.1 and 14.2 are based on an economic assessment from an “incremental cost to complete” perspective, which ignores any potential cancellation fees or other costs that would be incurred if the Project were stopped, as well as any fully-committed construction costs that would not be avoidable in the event the Project is cancelled.  If the results from the incremental cost to complete evaluation showed it was no longer cost-effective to pursue completing the Units, a second cancellation assessment would be performed to determine the economic value of canceling the Units. A cancellation assessment can provide the most appropriate perspective for deciding whether to cancel the Units as it would include the impacts of any cancellation fees or other costs associated with cancelling the Project in the economic analysis.  However, because Tables 14.1 and 14.2 both reflect significant savings and benefits to customers from the incremental cost to complete perspective across a wide range of possible future fuel and carbon prices, a cancellation assessment is not warranted at this time.  

In the February 2010 stipulation in Docket No. 29849, the Company agreed to provide sensitivity studies for comparison purposes to the results provided in Table 14.2 in which total megawatt (“MW”) load is alternatively increased by 1,000 MW and decreased by 1,000 MW.  These sensitivity study results are provided in Table 14.3 and Table 14.4, respectively.

In addition to the two sensitivity studies provided in Table 14.3 and 14.4, the Company also provided a sensitivity study based on the most recently available US DOE Energy Information Administration (“EIA”) natural gas forecast.  Table 14.5 contains results from a sensitivity study in which natural gas prices from the EIA Annual Energy Outlook 2011 were used.  The EIA gas prices assume no carbon costs.  For this study, the Company added carbon to the production costs to develop the $10, $20, and $30 CO2 cases.  The Company does not endorse the use of the EIA forecast sensitivity study for decision making purposes.
